title: Career roadmap · Legal Scholar
summary: Build an academic career at the intersection of technology law, artificial intelligence, data protection, digital rights and regulatory governance.

facts.Timeline assumption: The roadmap treats 2026 as the starting point and assumes the student is undertaking or has recently entered the Ph.D. stage. The first phase focuses on original research, doctrinal depth and publication; later phases build academic reputation, teaching, research leadership and interdisciplinary work.

horizons.question: What can I enter now?
horizons.output: Technology-law researcher, AI-governance researcher, data-protection researcher, legal research fellow or early-career legal scholar.

horizons.question: How should I specialise?
horizons.output: A recognised research niche in AI regulation, data protection, platform governance, digital rights, cybersecurity law or technology policy.

horizons.question: How should I evolve?
horizons.output: Established scholar with sustained publications, teaching, research collaborations, funded projects and policy engagement.

horizons.question: How can I remain relevant?
horizons.output: Research leadership covering new AI systems, automated decision-making, digital identity, privacy, cybersecurity and emerging technology regulation.

blocks.label: Career progression
blocks.text: Ph.D. Researcher → Technology Law Research Fellow → Postdoctoral Researcher → Assistant Professor → Associate Professor → Professor → Technology Law Research Centre Director → Senior/Distinguished Legal Scholar

blocks.label: Typical years
blocks.text:
2026–2030 → doctoral researcher and publication building
2030–2035 → postdoctoral/early faculty stage
2035–2040 → established technology-law scholar
2040–2046 → senior professor/research leader
Ph.D./research routes

The field will continue to change faster than traditional legal categories. A durable academic profile should therefore combine rigorous legal doctrine with enough technical understanding to interrogate AI systems, data flows, automated decision-making and cybersecurity practices. Research leadership should increasingly connect law with computer science, economics, ethics and international regulatory coordination.
